headline_marked: [[Modder transforms NAS into gaming PC]] with RTX 5060, boosts frame rate by 828% and breaks CPU world record
headline: Modder transforms NAS into gaming PC with RTX 5060, boosts frame rate by 828% and breaks CPU world record
summary: A YouTube enthusiast converted a ZimaCube 2 NAS into a gaming powerhouse, achieving an 828% frame rate increase in some titles and setting a Time Spy world record for its Intel Core i5-1235U CPU.
details: YouTube PC enthusiast TrashBench successfully modded a ZimaCube 2 NAS into a gaming PC, integrating an RTX 5060 graphics card. This extreme modification resulted in an astronomical 828% improvement in gaming performance in some titles. It also broke the Time Spy world record for the Intel Core i5-1235U CPU.

The ZimaCube 2 NAS is powered by an Intel Core i5-1235U, an Alder Lake chip with two P-cores and eight E-cores, along with Iris Xe integrated graphics. This system was never designed for gaming, but its motherboard features a vacant PCIe 4.0 x16 slot, making it a prime candidate for TrashBench's unconventional modifications.

Initial tests with the integrated Iris Xe graphics yielded poor results: 18 FPS in Hitman 3, 13 FPS in Cyberpunk 2077, and 31 FPS in Shadow of the Tomb Raider, all at 1080p low settings. Even adding an AMD Radeon Pro WX5100 workstation GPU only provided a 40% average boost, still not making games truly playable.

TrashBench then connected an RTX 5060 to the x16 slot using a riser cable, letting it hang outside the case due to its size. A 3D-printed frame and zip ties secured the GPU, creating a functional if unpolished setup for benchmarking.

To power the RTX 5060, all hard drive caddies were removed from the NAS, making space for a 750W SFX power supply. This dedicated PSU was hidden within the drive bay, with an extension cable running to the GPU's power connector, all concealed by the magnetic front cover.

Retesting showed dramatic improvements: Hitman 3 jumped to 167 FPS (827% increase), Cyberpunk 2077 hit 90 FPS (7x boost), and Shadow of the Tomb Raider reached 124 FPS (4x increase). The system delivered truly playable frame rates across the board.

Further attempts to improve performance by freezing the CPU proved ineffective, as the chip was not throttling and the GPU was already bottlenecked. This indicated the server-grade silicon had reached its maximum potential within this configuration.

Despite the impressive technical feat, the ZimaCube 2 starts at $1,299, making it an expensive base for a gaming PC. The system also lacks Windows and requires the iGPU's display output to be active for the dGPU to function, highlighting its server-first design.
